title: Large Language Models for Mental Health Applications: Systematic Review
study_design: PRISMA-guided systematic review of peer-reviewed literature on LLMs in mental health; searched MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, JMIR, and ACM Digital Library; included studies published from January 1, 2017 to April 30, 2024
population: Studies on large language models applied to mental health, including text-based screening for depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation, mental health conversational agents, and broader clinical/educational mental health applications
country_or_setting: International literature across digital mental health, social media, clinical transcript, conversational agent, and psychiatry-related settings
ai_type_application: Large language models (LLMs) for mental health applications including detection/screening of mental health conditions and suicidal ideation from text, mental health conversational agents, clinical decision support, treatment planning, medication guidance, education, and therapy enhancement
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to or application of LLMs such as BERT and variants, GPT models including ChatGPT/GPT-4, LaMDA, ERNIE Bot, LLaMA and related transformer-based models in mental health contexts
comparator_control_group: Varied across included studies; examples include convolutional neural networks, long short-term memory networks, baseline sentiment models, human analysts, physicians, chief physicians, psychologists, Google Search, and mental health professionals; no single unified comparator
mental_health_outcome: Depression detection, anxiety detection, social anxiety, loneliness, generalized anxiety, sentiment/emotion classification, suicidal ideation detection, empathy/acceptability of conversational agents, psychiatric diagnosis accuracy, treatment planning quality, medication advice quality, and broader clinical usefulness/safety in mental health
outcome_measurement_tool: Varied by included study; examples mentioned include F1-score, accuracy, precision, mean absolute error, relevance/human-like/empathy ratings, Patient Health Questionnaire-8 score prediction, vignette-based professional agreement, and examination accuracy
positive_effects: LLMs showed good effectiveness in detecting mental health issues and suicidal ideation from text, often outperforming some traditional deep learning methods. They may provide accessible, destigmatized, convenient, personalized, and cost-effective support, with nonjudgmental and empathic interactions. Some studies found strong performance in psychiatric case interpretation, exam-style questions, and agreement with mental health professionals on prognosis/treatment recommendations.
negative_effects_harms: Risks include inconsistent responses, hallucinations, biased or discriminatory outputs, lack of clinical judgment, inability to reliably handle emergencies, harmful or inappropriate recommendations, overestimation of suicide risk in some contexts, privacy and confidentiality concerns, black-box interpretability problems, dehumanization of care, possible overreliance by patients and clinicians, and lack of a benchmarked ethical framework.
evidence_type: Systematic review of heterogeneous primary studies and review articles
main_finding: LLMs have substantial potential in mental health for early screening, conversational support, and selected clinical aid functions, but current evidence indicates that risks and unresolved ethical/technical issues likely outweigh benefits for routine clinical use. The review concludes LLMs should not replace professional mental health services and are not yet ready for widespread clinical implementation.
effect_size_key_result: Among 40 included articles, 15 addressed detection of mental health conditions/suicidal ideation, 7 covered conversational agents, and 18 covered other applications/evaluations. Example results cited include GPT-3.5 F1-score 0.78 for depression detection versus CNN 0.53-0.59; RoBERTa for depression severity prediction with MAE 3.65 on PHQ-8; Emotion-aware BERT Tiny accuracy 93.14% for sentiment and 85.46% for emotion analysis; PsychBERT F1-score 0.63 versus CNN 0.57 and LSTM 0.51; BERTimbau for suicidal ideation accuracy 0.955, precision 0.961, F1-score 0.954; ChatGPT mean empathy 3.64 versus physicians 3.13; ChatGPT answered 85% of neurology board-style questions versus average human performance 73.8%.
limitations_bias: The review notes heterogeneity across datasets, models, and methods, making horizontal comparison difficult. Most included studies used social media data, which may introduce age and language bias and underrepresent older adults and non-English-speaking populations. Limited multilingual, expert-annotated datasets were available. Most identified studies focused on BERT/GPT, limiting diversity of LLMs reviewed. Rapid model evolution means findings may quickly become outdated. The paper reports Cohen kappa of 0.84 for screening agreement and use of Risk of Bias 2, but also included review articles due to limited literature, adding heterogeneity.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a comprehensive systematic review summarizing both beneficial and harmful effects of AI/LLMs on mental health applications, including impacts on detection, support, empathy, safety, and ethical concerns.
reason_for_decision: Directly addresses AI effects in mental health, synthesizes 40 studies on LLM applications, reports positive and negative impacts, and is highly relevant background evidence for a systematic review on AI effects on mental health.
notes_for_research_question: This is a review rather than a primary causal study. Useful for mapping application areas, benefits, harms, and evidence gaps. It emphasizes that current evidence does not support replacing clinicians and that clinical risks may exceed benefits. Particularly relevant for identifying adverse effects such as hallucinations, inconsistency, privacy risks, emergency-response limitations, and overreliance, as well as benefits like accessibility, destigmatization, empathy, and text-based screening performance.
